name: Kankanaey
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Allen, Lawrence P. 1975. Distinctive features in Kankanaey. Philippine Journal of Linguistics 6(2): 23-30. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 25830; Kibungan, Benguet dialect.)
catalog_locator: Sec. 1.2 'Stress within the phonological word', p. 23; phonetic correlates p. 24; sec. 5 'Tentative orthography', p. 29.
catalog_quote: In the phonological word one syllable bears major stress, the other syllables a lesser degree of stress. Stress always falls on one of the last three syllables, but within these three syllables its placement is unpredictable. In some cases its position is the minimal difference between a pair of words, e.g., ʔótot 'rat'; ʔotót 'flatulence'; sáʔoŋ 'adze', saʔóŋ 'canine tooth'; manbálin 'to travel', manbalín 'to become'. [p. 24] The phonological constituents of stress are prolongation of the syllable peak, increase in volume, and rise in pitch. These constituents, however, are highly susceptible to higher level intonational pressures. [p. 29] Although stress is not predictable, it is omitted from the tentative orthography for three reasons: 1) very few word pairs are distinguished by stress only; 2) stress is not marked in Pilipino, although it is also phonemic in that language; and 3) in initial reading tests, the readers had no difficulty in placing stress properly, even though stress was not indicated in the written text.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical/contrastive: each phonological word has one primary stress located within a three-syllable final window (antepenult, penult or ultima), its position not predictable by rule and distinguishing minimal pairs. Per Allen 1977: 283, affixable roots carry stress only on one of the last two syllables (antepenult stress is confined to a few unaffixable roots), and stress shifts one syllable rightward under suffixation for most root shapes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only that non-primary syllables bear 'a lesser degree of stress' (1975: 23); no secondary-stress rule given. Allen 1977/1980/2021 describe gemination of the onset of the pre-stress syllable when two open syllables precede the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under suffixation does not apply to roots of shape CV(C), CVC.CV, CVC.CVC (unless final vowel is e), CVC.CVC.CVC (Allen 1977: 282; 1980: 28); stress shifts left onto ma-/na-/ka- with monosyllabic stative roots; stress may not precede a root-medial consonant+glottal cluster (1977: 283). Stress correlates 'highly susceptible to higher level intonational pressures' (1975: 24). Few minimal pairs per 1975: 29, but 'many minimal pairs' per the 2021 dictionary.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, which includes enclitic pronouns (1975 sec. 1.1, e.g. ʔasáwam 'your wife', pinádasko 'I tried'). Dialect: Kibungan, Benguet (Kibungan to Bakun). Stress unmarked in practical orthography; marked with acute in the 2021 dictionary.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Lawrence Allen papers and the 2021 Webonary dictionary describe the Kankanaey of Kibungan, Benguet Province (area Kibungan north to Bakun), i.e. Central Kankanaey = Glottolog kank1243 / ISO kne, the target. Not to be confused with Northern Kankanay (Sagada; ISO xnn, Glottolog nort2877), for which Reid 1971 (data Hettick 1966) separately lists stress as phonemic, and which is probably the 'Kankanay' of Zorc's 1993 class-A list.

new_statements.quote: The acute accent is used to mark the stressed vowel of words having more than one syllable. Vowels so marked should be pronounced with a slight increase in volume, and when they occur in open syllables, they should also be lengthened. Many minimal pairs occur in which stress is the only distinguishing factor, e.g., ótot, 'rat', otót 'flatulence'; dáan 'old', daán 'not yet'. Stress is not marked in the practical orthography. [...] Stress Shift. Stress shifts one syllable to the right upon suffixation of roots with syllable patterns other than ĆV́(C) and CVC.CV́. With roots having the pattern CVC.CV́C, stress shift occurs only when the final vowel of the root is e.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog's existing statement (Allen 1975: stress within the last three syllables, placement unpredictable, minimal pairs): contrastive, lexically marked stress. Adds the phonetic correlates (intensity, plus length in open syllables), the orthographic practice (marked in the dictionary, not in the practical orthography), and the morphologically conditioned Stress Shift rule under affixation. The dictionary's own 'Grammatical information' page shows all cited headwords stress-marked (daké, kittóy, andó, kasisíyek, makabéteng), 175 accented forms on that page alone, but states no placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive and lexically specified: every polysyllabic headword carries an acute accent on its stressed vowel because placement cannot be read off the word (minimal pairs ótot/otót, dáan/daán). Phonetically the stressed vowel is louder and, in an open syllable, lengthened. Under suffixation stress moves one syllable rightward except for roots shaped (C)V́(C) or CVC.CV́ (and CVC.CV́C roots only when the final vowel is e); under ma-/na-/ka- prefixation of monosyllabic stative roots it moves one syllable leftward, staying on the root when prefix and suffix co-occur.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress Shift does not apply to roots of shape (C)V́(C) or CVC.CV́ (éken, pok-ían, kibtóten); CVC.CV́C roots shift only when the final vowel is e (padsekán); with prefix+suffix combined, stress stays on the root.
new_statements.identity_note: The Allen materials (dictionary, 1975/1977/1980 papers, J. Allen grammar) describe the Kankanaey [kne] of Kibungan, Benguet. The Reid 1971 excerpt sitting in the same check folder is Northern Kankanay [xnn] (nort2877), a different language, and was not used.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Work 1 (Allen 2014 / dissertation 2011): no word-stress statement was missed in the 2011 text; the only prosody remark not reported by the compiler is ch. 7 sec. 7.1.1 (Information Structure, p. ~2 of the chapter file), 'speakers do not use special prosodic intensity to highlight focus elements', which is about focus marking, not word stress. The real miss is bibliographic: the 2014 edition and its 2019 ePub carry 'Appendix A Phonology and Morphophonology of Kankanaey' (SIL records 58812 and 82404), absent from the 2011 dissertation, so that work is a likely stress source that remains unopened (both records 'Not Available Online').
